name: PCI DSS v4.0
reference: PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement 2.2.7 (non-console administrative access) and 4.2.1 (strong cryptography and security protocols), with the Appendix G glossary definition of 'Strong Cryptography' (verified against the source document, internal reference copy, estandares/pci-ssc/)
summary: Strong cryptography as PCI defines it: 'key lengths that provide a minimum of 112-bits of effective key strength and proper key-management practices'.
notes: The PCI SSC glossary names no SSH algorithms; it defines strong cryptography by reference to NIST SP 800-57 Part 1, BSI TR-02102-1, ECRYPT-CSA D5.4 and ISO/IEC 18033, so the exclusions below are derived from those. The same entry adds: 'It is recommended that all new implementations use a minimum of 128-bits of effective key strength', which this profile reports rather than enforces, since it is a recommendation and not the floor. Requirement 12.3.3 also demands a documented inventory of the cipher suites and protocols in use: the JSON report serves as that inventory.

host_key.reason: SHA-1 signatures are no longer industry-accepted, so they do not meet the strong cryptography definition.

cipher.reason: RC4 and DES fall below 112-bit strength; three-key Triple DES lost NIST approval at the end of 2023 and is therefore no longer industry-accepted.

mac.reason: MD5 is broken and tags shorter than 112 bits fall below the strong cryptography floor.

kex.reason: 1024-bit key establishment provides about 80-bit strength, below the 112-bit floor.
